samples.text:
These days, a lot of universities are using online courses instead of the traditional classes in a classroom. This trend has both advantages and disadvantages, and I will discuss them in this essay.

The first advantage is that online courses are very flexible. Students can watch the lectures at any time and in any place, so they can study and work at the same time. This is very helpful for students who has a part-time job or a family to look after. Another advantage is the cost. Students do not need to pay for transport or rent a room near the university, so they can save a lot of money. Also, universities can teach more students because they do not need big lecture halls.

However, there are also some disadvantages of online learning. Firstly, students do not have much contact with their teachers and classmates. In a classroom, they can ask questions immediately and discuss about ideas with other students, but online it is more difficult. As a result, some students feel lonely and lose their motivation. Secondly, not every students have a good computer or a fast internet connection, especially in the countryside. This means that some students cannot follow the lessons properly. Finally, some subjects like medicine or engineering need practical work in a laboratory, and this is not possible on a screen.

In conclusion, online courses are flexible and cheap, and they help many people to study who could not go to university before. But they also reduce the communication between students and teachers and they are not suitable for all subject. I think universities should use a mix of both online and classroom teaching.
samples.why: Addresses both advantages and disadvantages · relevant but list-like ideas with limited development · mechanical sequencing (Firstly, Secondly, Finally) · adequate vocabulary · several agreement and preposition errors.

samples.text:
Across the world, a growing number of universities are moving their teaching from lecture theatres to digital platforms. This shift brings real benefits in terms of access and flexibility, but it also raises concerns about the quality of learning and the student experience.

One major advantage of online courses is that they make higher education available to people who would otherwise be excluded. Mature students with full-time jobs, parents with young children and those living far from a campus can all follow lectures at a time and place that suits them. In addition, recorded lessons allows learners to pause, replay and review difficult material at their own pace, which can be particularly helpful for those studying in a second language. From the institution's point of view, digital delivery reduces the need for expensive buildings, and these savings could be passed on to students through lower fees.

On the other hand, replacing classrooms entirely has significant drawbacks. Face-to-face teaching allows lecturers to notice when students are confused and adapt their explanations immediately, while online, many learners simply stop engaging without anyone realising. The social side of university is also lost: discussions with classmates, study groups and informal conversations with tutors all contribute to both learning and wellbeing, and these are hard to reproduce through a screen. Furthermore, practical subjects such as nursing, chemistry or architecture depend on hands-on work that cannot be done remotely.

A further problem is that online study demands a high level of self-discipline. Younger students who have just left school often struggle to organise their time without the structure of regular classes, and they may fall behind as a result.

In conclusion, online courses widen access and offer valuable flexibility, but they weaken interaction and are unsuitable for practical disciplines. For this reason, a blended approach is likely to serve most students better than a complete move away from the classroom.
samples.why: Both sides clearly presented with extended support · clear central topic in each paragraph · range of cohesive devices · good collocation (widen access, hands-on work) · frequent error-free sentences, one agreement slip.

samples.text:
The steady replacement of lecture halls with virtual classrooms is one of the most visible changes in higher education in recent years. Although this trend has made university study more accessible and adaptable, it also risks diluting some of the most valuable aspects of a traditional education.

The principal benefit of online provision is its capacity to widen participation. Because lectures can be accessed from anywhere, students in remote regions, those with disabilities that make travel difficult and adults balancing study with employment are no longer disadvantaged by geography or rigid timetables. Digital materials are also more flexible as learning tools: a recorded lecture can be revisited before an examination, subtitled or slowed down, giving learners greater control over how they absorb information. For universities, meanwhile, online delivery allows a single course to reach thousands of students without a corresponding increase in staff or facilities.

Yet these gains come at a cost. Learning at university is not merely the transfer of information; it is also shaped by debate, questioning and collaboration, which tend to flourish in shared physical spaces. In a live seminar, a tutor can challenge a weak argument or draw a quiet student into the discussion, whereas in an online forum such interaction is often delayed, superficial or absent altogether. Isolation is a related concern, as students who rarely meet their peers may feel less connected to their institution and more likely to abandon their studies. There are practical limitations too: laboratory work, clinical training and studio-based design cannot be meaningfully replicated at a distance.

Equally important is the issue of unequal access to technology. A course delivered entirely online assumes a reliable device and a stable internet connection, which not every student can take for granted.

In summary, online courses offer flexibility, reach and efficiency, but at the expense of interaction, community and practical training. The most effective universities are likely to be those that combine digital tools with meaningful face-to-face teaching rather than abandoning the classroom altogether.
samples.why: Sufficiently addresses both advantages and disadvantages with well-developed, relevant support · logical sequencing and well-managed paragraphs · wide, precise vocabulary used flexibly · wide range of accurate structures.
